title: Loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery using fusion networks
authors: Felix Burt, Richard Meister, Sheng-Ku Lin, Kuan-Cheng Chen, Michael Hanks, Roberto Bondesan, M. S. Kim, Kin K. Leung
abstract: Networking matter-based quantum processing units (QPUs) offers a promising route to scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers. This requires distributed logical operations to be performed across photonic links, where noise is characteristically different from and stronger than in local QPUs owing to photon loss and probabilistic linear-optical operations. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are designed to be robust against loss and probabilistic photonic operations, suggesting they could complement circuit-based error correction at the interface between networked QPUs. We use ZX calculus transformations to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols and apply them to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery, demonstrating that several protocols attain a $50\%$ interface-erasure threshold when local noise is absent, including circuit-based lattice surgery using fused Bell pairs and hybrid protocols using linear cluster states. Relative to a straight Bell-pair interface geometry, the hybrid protocols increase the merge-observable interface distance from $d+1$ to $2d+1$ and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ to $d$. We calculate how the threshold decreases when using truncated resource states and map correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. We then convert these erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds and probe subthreshold performance using fusion boosting. At circuit and resource-state error rates of $10^{-3}$, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage. As local noise is reduced to $10^{-4}$ and below, the linear-chain protocols improve more rapidly with decreasing erasure, suggesting that interface distance enhancements are effective in low local noise regimes.
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of scaling quantum computers by analyzing error correction for distributed lattice surgery across noisy photonic links. The authors develop and test hybrid protocols that combine circuit-based and measurement-based techniques. They demonstrate that these hybrid approaches significantly enhance the error-correcting distance of the quantum interface, especially in low-noise regimes.
main_problem: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computation requires performing distributed logical operations across photonic links, which suffer from noise like photon loss, unlike local QPUs.
main_result: Hybrid protocols significantly improve the interface distance for distributed lattice surgery, achieving a 50% erasure threshold when local noise is negligible.
method: The authors use ZX calculus transformations to construct and analyze hybrid syndrome extraction protocols applied to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery.
model_or_system: The work models matter-based Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) connected via photonic links, implementing lattice surgery for distributed operations and analyzing performance under a heterogeneous error model.
key_observables: Interface-erasure threshold, merge-observable interface distance, and perpendicular-observable interface distance.
important_parameters: Local error rates ($10^{-3}$ and $10^{-4}$), and the degree of resource state truncation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to model the combination of circuit noise, resource-state errors, and photonic loss/fusion failures, treating losses as erasures.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the construction process from the logical level down to a hybrid realization involving fusion networks at the interface and circuit-based syndrome extraction elsewhere.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem of distributed noise, detailing the use of ZX calculus and Pauli webs, applying these tools to compare different interface geometries (fused Bell pairs vs. fusion networks), and finally analyzing performance under realistic, combined noise models.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, quantifiable improvements to the fault-tolerance thresholds for networking quantum processors, which is crucial for building large-scale quantum computers using photonic interconnects.

At the logical level the merge implements a joint measurement, whose outcome carries the joint observable (red web). This maps to an abstract syndrome extraction diagram with Pauli webs corresponding to logical observables and detecting regions (Section III). Using web-preserving transformations (Section III B) the seam is split and transformed into a graph-like sub-diagram (Section IV C 1) which can be split into resource state components. FIG. 2: Node types. The four values of the type map t, together with the bold leg of a classical output. Spiders are drawn green (Z) and red (X) and carry a phase α ∈{0, π}; Hadamard nodes have degree two, while ports and classical outputs degree one. For the standard ZX calculus and ZX-instrument conventions, see Refs. [64, 69].

FIG. 4: Syndrome extraction diagrams and their Pauli webs. (a) Phase-free projector gadgets for a four-qubit Z-type generator and a two-qubit X-type generator, each with a generator spider joined to data spiders. Exchanging spider colours exchanges the generator type. (b) All consecutive measurements of the same Pauli type can be merged into a single layer, and composing layers gives a syndrome extraction diagram (SED), with detecting regions, stabilisers, and logical webs corresponding to the code. A Z-type detecting region is shown in red, an X-type stabiliser from a two-qubit boundary generator in green, and an X logical web along the top boundary in green.
FIG. 5: Splitting a detecting region. (left) An SED with a selected region S and a highlighted detecting region. (right) Splitting the boundary generator spiders gives D[S] a matching boundary.

FIG. 6: Two realisations of the syndrome extraction diagram: circuit-based (a) and measurement-based (b). In the circuit-based realisation, directed edges represent data-qubit world-lines, while each generator spider lies on a distinct world-line and has a classical output recording its stabiliser measurement outcome. In the measurement-based realisation, each bulk spider lies on a distinct world-line and represents a qubit initialised in |+⟩, while edges represent CZ gates forming a cluster state and classical outputs record the measurement outcomes.
